solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Monk(ey)

parts.note: the bracket lets the clue be read two ways: a friar of a Franciscan order, and a South American primate named after that friar's hood

explanation.surface: A bare word with a bracketed tail, as if a dictionary entry could not make up its mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with the bracket ignored, the clue says Monk; read with it, Monkey. One name covers both: a Franciscan friar and the small primate whose dark cap looks like his cowl.
explanation.definitionFit: The Franciscan friars of that order and the cowled-looking South American primate share one name, so both readings point to it.

clue.text: Oddly, crowd goes last to cheer the old man

indicators.note: oddly takes the odd-positioned letters of crowd and of goes
last to points to the final letter of the word cheer

explanation.surface: A crowd drifts off and is the last to cheer the old man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' gives C, O, D from CROWD and G, E from GOES; 'last to' adds the R ending CHEER.
explanation.definitionFit: A codger is an informal word for an elderly fellow, often eccentric.

clue.text: Fine perhaps like some wordplay on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: wordplay that is like a pun could be called punnish

explanation.surface: A broadcaster fined for being too fond of puns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine perhaps' is the definition by example: a fine is one way to penalise someone. 'on the radio' signals the sound of PUNNISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Fining someone is one example of penalising them for wrongdoing.

clue.text: Gather ye rosebuds for another mad recipe

indicators.note: another hints at a different version of the letters of mad recipe

explanation.surface: A line of old poetry offered as an alternative to a crazy cooking recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder: 'another' rearranges all of MAD RECIPE. Herrick's line 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may' carries the same message as the Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace's Latin motto means seize the day, the same urging as Herrick's poem to enjoy youth while it lasts.

clue.text: Modulate and polllute?

indicators.note: the question mark flags that the misspelt word is itself the instruction: its stray letter is to be put inside the word it should be

parts.note: the word as printed reads as pollute, which means infect
the printed word carries one surplus letter beyond pollute, and that spare letter is the piece put inside

explanation.surface: A question about whether changing a voice could spoil it.
explanation.walkthrough: The deliberate typo 'polllute' is the whole wordplay: read as pollute it gives INFECT, and its surplus L goes inside, just as the misspelling carries an L too many.
explanation.definitionFit: To inflect the voice is to vary its pitch or tone, which is to modulate it.

clue.text: Keep quiet about warm coat

indicators.note: the letters for keep quiet are placed around the other piece, as 'about' means surrounding

parts.note: an instruction to keep quiet is SH
warmth is heat

explanation.surface: Someone is told to say nothing about a cosy winter coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like the definition, but it belongs with 'quiet' to make SH, which goes 'about' HEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting covering, a protective layer wrapped round something, so a coat in that sense.

clue.text: Mustang's tool may be a lucky thing

parts.note: a mustang is a wild horse, so mustang's is horse's
a hoe is a garden tool

explanation.surface: A wild horse's equipment might bring good fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mustang's tool' reads as one piece of horse kit, but the possessive gives a plural-looking word and the tool is a gardener's. 'may be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The iron shoe of a horse is a traditional good-luck charm hung over doors.

clue.text: Hall isn't built to provide accommodation for colonies

indicators.note: built means the letters of Hall isn't are constructed into a new form

explanation.surface: A hall that was never built to house colonists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'colonies' suggests settlers, but here they are colonies of insects.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounds built by ants house their insect colonies.

clue.text: Eats greens? We hear they're no longer effective

indicators.note: we hear means the sound of the phrase is what counts

parts.note: someone who eats greens has beans

explanation.surface: A health tip: vegetable eaters, apparently, lose their edge.
explanation.definitionFit: People whose best days are over, once successful but now past it.

clue.text: Ultimately cod as well as other fish shedding scales

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word cod

parts.note: as well as means and
the ruff is a different fish from the cod, a small perch

explanation.surface: A fishmonger's list: cod in the end, plus some other fish, being descaled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shedding scales' reads as fish being cleaned, but it is the definition of flakes from the scalp.
explanation.definitionFit: Dandruff is the flaking skin people lose from the scalp, little scales being shed.

clue.text: String instrument returned without charge

parts.note: G is a string, as in the G string of a violin or guitar

indicators.note: returned means the word for the instrument is read backwards

parts.note: a sitar is an Indian stringed instrument

explanation.surface: A stringed instrument sent back free of charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String instrument' looks like one idea, but 'String' alone gives G and 'instrument' is SITAR, turned back to RATIS by 'returned'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis is Latin-derived English for free, given without any payment asked.

clue.text: Leading optician gets labelled Eagle Eye

indicators.note: leading takes the first letter of each of the following four words

explanation.surface: An optician earns the nickname Eagle Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eagle Eye' looks like a single nickname, but 'Eagle' gives its E to the initials and 'Eye' is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to stare at someone, so to eye them.

clue.text: Unfairly segregate seasonal fare

indicators.note: unfairly suggests the letters of segregate are dealt with wrongly, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint about seasonal food being handed out to people kept unjustly apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfairly segregate' reads as a social protest; 'Unfairly' is the anagram signal on SEGREGATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A chocolate egg eaten at the spring festival is food tied to one time of year.

clue.text: Diet drug in top drawer?

parts.note: E is short for ecstasy, the drug
lite is the low-calorie labelling word for diet food

explanation.surface: A slimming drug in the top drawer of a bathroom cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'Diet drug' as an E-LITE pill: E for the drug ecstasy, LITE for diet. 'top drawer' is the definition, not a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Top drawer is an idiom for the very best class of people or things, the cream.

clue.text: Symbolic figure, motherless northerner

indicators.note: motherless says the word for mother, ma, is dropped from the figure

parts.note: a mascot is a figure that symbolises a team or event

explanation.surface: A lone northern figure, an orphan, standing for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'motherless' takes MA (mother) from MASCOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Scotland lives in the far north of Britain, so a northerner.

clue.text: Pretend agony in speech bubbles

indicators.note: in speech means the phrase is spoken aloud

parts.note: pretend is sham and agony is pain

explanation.surface: Fake suffering voiced in a cartoon's speech bubbles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speech bubbles' looks like a single cartoon term, but 'in speech' signals the sound of SHAM PAIN and 'bubbles' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubbly is the informal name for sparkling wine, so bubbles here.

clue.text: The man's into clone reproduction in class

indicators.note: into means the pronoun for the man goes inside the other letters
a reproduction remakes the letters of clone in a new order

parts.note: the man is he

explanation.surface: A man joining a cloning experiment, inside a classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reproduction' rearranges the letters of clone to ECLON, and 'into' puts the pronoun inside after its C; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a level or rank in an organisation, a grade of people.

clue.text: Proper interaction with threat as article of faith

indicators.note: interaction suggests the letters of two pieces mixed together to make a third

explanation.surface: A formal treaty that turns a threat into a matter of belief.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse anagram: the answer mixed ('interaction') with THREAT gives the letters of ARTICLE OF FAITH.
explanation.definitionFit: Something official is authorised and properly done, as in proper channels.

clue.text: Nip back after funds were stripped to give support

indicators.note: after puts the reversed piece at the end
stripped means the outer letters of funds and of were are peeled off
back means the word nip is read the other way

explanation.surface: A quick trip back after the money has run out, to help someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped' works on both words, peeling each one's first and last letters; 'back' turns the short word round, and 'after' places it at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To underpin is to put a firm foundation beneath something, so to strengthen or back it.

clue.text: Sweet and affectionate worker

parts.note: affectionate means fond
an ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: A description of a kind and loving employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective in a list with 'affectionate', but it is a noun here: a confection.
explanation.definitionFit: Fondant is a soft sugar paste used as an icing or filling, a confection.

clue.text: Bird in the afternoon

indicators.note: in shows the letters are found inside the word afternoon

explanation.surface: A bird sighting in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is inside afTERNoon.
explanation.definitionFit: A tern is a seabird related to the gulls.

clue.text: See 3
Record of tramp embracing setter

indicators.note: embracing means the vagrant's letters hold the setter's letter

parts.note: a dosser is a homeless person, a vagrant
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A file kept on a homeless person who hugs the crossword compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is I, held by DOSSER, British slang for a rough sleeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A dossier is a file of documents about a person or subject, a written account.

clue.text: Local green tea infusion

indicators.note: an infusion puts the letter for tea into the other word, as tea is infused

parts.note: green means inexperienced, naive
T is short for tea

explanation.surface: A local blend of green tea being brewed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green tea' looks like a drink, but 'green' is NAIVE and 'tea' is T, put in by 'infusion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A native is a person born in a place, someone local to it.

clue.text: Fly like Michael Jackson said

definitions.meaning: to fly is to run away quickly, to scram
the title of a 1983 Michael Jackson hit telling someone to get lost

explanation.surface: A dance move flown in the style of Michael Jackson.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are an order to clear off, which Michael Jackson sang as a song title.

clue.text: Freeze alloy with metals to make time capsule

indicators.note: an alloy mixes metals together, so the letters are blended and some are set aside

explanation.surface: Making a frozen time capsule out of an alloy of several metals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alloy' says the letters of TIME CAPSULE are a mixture of METALS plus the answer: take out M, E, T, A, L, S and I, C, P, U, E are left to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice up is to become covered in ice, frozen over.

clue.text: Once more appear sure about farce, perhaps

indicators.note: about means the letters of sure are turned around into another order
perhaps hints that farce stands for one possible arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A playwright's farce coming back on stage, sure enough.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams: 'about' works on SURE to give RESU, and 'perhaps' on FARCE to give RFACE.
explanation.definitionFit: To resurface is to come back into view after being gone, to show up again.

clue.text: Alter dance again?

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
a jig is a lively dance

explanation.surface: Changing a dance by performing it once more.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as RE-JIG, the answer means 'dance again'.
explanation.definitionFit: To rejig is to rearrange or adjust something, to change it.

clue.text: Hang up mirror section, backing challenge

indicators.note: backing means the section is read in the opposite direction
a section of the words Hang up mirror is taken out of them

explanation.surface: A DIY instruction to hang a mirror section on a backing board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'section' takes NGUPMI from 'haNG UP MIrror'; 'backing' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To impugn a claim is to call it into question, to dispute it.

clue.text: The odds on Janis and idiot perhaps to break up

indicators.note: perhaps shows the letters may be put in another order
the odds means the odd-numbered letters of Janis are taken

explanation.surface: A bookmaker's odds on Janis and an idiot splitting up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The odds on' looks like betting talk but takes J, N, S from JANIS; 'perhaps' then rearranges those with IDIOT.
explanation.definitionFit: To disjoint is to take apart at the joints, so to separate or dismember.

clue.text: Support from artificial intelligence

indicators.note: from shows the letters are taken out of the phrase artificial intelligence

explanation.surface: Getting support from a computer that can think.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across the two words: artificiaL INTELligence.
explanation.definitionFit: A lintel is the horizontal beam over a door or window that bears the wall above.

clue.text: Piece in the paper about Steptoe and son

indicators.note: about means the newspaper's letters go around the other piece

parts.note: FT, the Financial Times, is the paper this puzzle appears in
Steptoe and Son was a British TV sitcom about a father and son who were rag-and-bone men, so rag men

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about the old TV comedy Steptoe and Son.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about a father and son who collected scrap and old clothes in a horse-drawn cart; the paper is the Financial Times, where the puzzle ran.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragment is a small broken-off part of something, a bit or piece.
